title: Introduction to Modal Verbs (Extended): The Power of Auxiliary Verbs
description: Explore modal auxiliary verbs in depth — their grammar rules, core meanings, real-world uses in signs and speech, and how modals shift certainty, obligation, and permission in everyday English.
author: AST English Academy

props.content: Welcome to the World of Modal Verbs

Compare these two sentences: 'You must hand in your essay today' versus 'You might hand in your essay today.' The main verb (hand in) stays the same — but the tiny helper word before it completely changes the force, expectation, and tone. These helper words are modal auxiliary verbs, and mastering them is one of the most powerful skills in English writing and speaking.

props.title: Why Modals Matter
props.content: Modal verbs let you fine-tune meaning without rewriting an entire sentence. They express attitude — certainty, obligation, permission, ability, and advice — in just one or two words.

props.question: Which sentence sounds the most forceful to you?

options.text: You MUST submit the assignment by 5 PM.
You SHOULD submit the assignment by 5 PM.
You COULD submit the assignment by 5 PM.
You MIGHT submit the assignment by 5 PM.

slides.title: What Exactly Is a Modal Verb?

props.content: A modal auxiliary verb (or simply modal) is a special type of helping verb that modifies the main verb in a sentence. Modals never stand alone — they always appear before a base verb (the verb without -ing, -ed, or -s). For example: She can swim, not She can swims.

items.title: Are modals the same as main verbs?
items.content: No. Main verbs carry the core action (run, write, eat). Modals modify that action by adding attitude — permission, obligation, possibility, etc. You cannot say 'I musted' or 'She cans' because modals never change form.

items.title: What is the most common modal error?
items.content: Adding -s, -ed, or -ing to a modal. Correct: 'He must go.' Incorrect: 'He musts go' or 'He must going.' The main verb stays in base form after every modal.

items.title: Do modals work in questions?
items.content: Yes. Modals invert with the subject in questions: 'Can you help me?' 'Must we leave now?' 'Should they revise the policy?'

props.statement: Modal verbs can be used alone without a main verb, e.g. 'She must.'
props.explanation: Modals require a main verb (usually in base form). 'She must leave' is correct; 'She must' alone is incomplete unless the verb is implied from context.

props.content: Three Key Characteristics of Every Modal

items: They always partner with a main base verb: must GO, can SWIM, should READ.
They never change form — no adding -ed, -ing, or -s to the modal itself.
They express attitudes: certainty, obligation, permission, ability, and advice.

questions.question: Which sentence follows correct modal grammar?
questions.explanation: 'Must' never takes -s, and the following verb stays in base form: 'complete'.

props.content: Core Modal Verbs and Their Primary Roles

English has nine core modals you will use constantly: can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, and would. Semi-modals like have to, ought to, and need to behave similarly but follow slightly different grammar patterns.

props.title: Core Modal Verbs — Flip Each Card

cards.back: Strict obligation or high certainty: 'You must stop at red lights.' 'I shall return tomorrow.'
Advice or strong recommendation: 'You should rest after exercise.'
Low possibility or polite suggestion: 'It might rain.' 'Could you help me?'
Ability or formal permission: 'She can swim.' 'May I leave early?'
Future certainty or polite requests: 'The bus will arrive soon.' 'Would you mind waiting?'

props.content: Explore Modal Messages in Everyday Life

Modal verbs appear everywhere — on school noticeboards, in library rules, weather forecasts, and polite conversations. Tap each hotspot below to inspect how a single modal word sets the tone of a real-world message.

props.title: Tap the Hotspots to Inspect How Modal Verbs Set Rules and Expectations

hotspots.label: Library Rule
hotspots.content: 'Silence MUST be maintained in the reading room.' — Modal 'must' makes silence non-negotiable; breaking this rule has consequences.

hotspots.label: Weather Forecast
hotspots.content: 'Temperatures MIGHT drop later this evening.' — Modal 'might' expresses possibility, not certainty. The forecast could change.

hotspots.label: Study Tip
hotspots.content: 'Students SHOULD take short breaks every 30 minutes.' — Modal 'should' offers helpful advice without forcing compliance.

hotspots.label: Permission Sign
hotspots.content: 'Visitors MAY use the guest Wi-Fi network.' — Modal 'may' grants formal permission to an allowed action.

props.content: Categorise Modal Verbs by What They Express

props.title: One Modal, Many Meanings
props.content: Some modals like 'must' can express obligation ('You must wear a helmet') OR logical deduction ('She must be tired — she ran a marathon'). Context tells you which meaning applies.

props.content: Sentence Structure: Subject + Modal + Base Verb

data: You should review your notes before class.
We might visit the museum on Tuesday.
She can speak three languages fluently.

props.statement: In the sentence 'He should studying harder', the modal grammar is correct.
props.explanation: After 'should', the main verb must stay in base form: 'He should study harder.' Never add -ing directly after a modal.

props.content: Modals as a Volume Dial for Certainty

Modal verbs act like a dial controlling how confident a speaker feels. At 100% certainty you hear will or must. At 70–80% you hear should. At 40–50% you hear may. At 10–30% you hear might or could. Explore the timeline below to see how certainty decreases step by step.

props.title: The Modal Certainty Spectrum (Highest to Lowest)

events.title: Will / Must
events.description: Absolute future fact or strong logical deduction: 'The sun will rise.' 'She must be exhausted.'

events.title: Should / Ought to
events.description: High expectation based on normal patterns: 'The train should arrive on time.'

events.title: May / Can
events.description: Moderate possibility or permission: 'We may go to the cinema later.'

events.title: Might / Could
events.description: Low, unproven speculation: 'It might snow next week.'

props.title: Select ALL True Statements About Modal Verbs

questions.question: Which statements about modal verbs are correct?

options.text: Modals are followed by base-form verbs
Modals take -ed endings in the past tense
Can and may can express permission

questions.explanation: Modals use base verbs and never take -ed. 'Can' and 'may' express permission. 'Must' expresses obligation or deduction, not ability.
